etymology: English given name Thomas, from the Aramaic t’oma, “twin”; with the Scottish surname Halyburton, a place-name of the Berwickshire lands of Halyburton.
biblical_def: Thomas Halyburton (1674–1712) was a Scottish divine, minister at Ceres and afterward Professor of Divinity at St Andrews, whose brief life burned with an uncommon nearness to God. Reared amid the sufferings of the persecuted Church of Scotland and driven for a season into the darkness of doubt, he was brought at length to a settled assurance that Christ, and Christ alone, is the ground of the sinner’s peace; and out of that recovery he wrote against the rising deism of his age, contending that natural religion cannot save and that the revealed gospel is the only remedy for a guilty conscience. His Memoirs, penned as a dying testimony to the free grace that had held him, were so savoury that George Whitefield prized them and the Wesleys commended them, for in them a soul lays bare its wrestlings and its rest. When he came to die he gathered his brethren and his household to watch the LORD carry a believer over Jordan, saying that he had a heaven already begun. His labour teaches that sound doctrine and warm experience are not rivals but one cord: he defended the faith with the mind of a scholar and clung to Christ with the heart of a child, and so left the Church a pattern of dying grace.
webster_summary: Scottish theologian and professor at St Andrews whose Memoirs of dying grace were prized by Whitefield and the Wesleys.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved not because Halyburton’s name is quarrelled over in the modern academy, but because the substance of his witness is nearly forgotten: that a man may argue the faith with rigour and yet die in the arms of a felt salvation, and that the two are not at war.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is assurance grounded in Christ’s finished work rather than in the shifting weather of the frame, together with a robust defence of revealed religion against every scheme that would set human reason above the Word of God.

etymology: English given name John, from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious”; with the surname Willison, a patronymic, “son of Will,” a diminutive of William.
biblical_def: John Willison (1680–1750) was minister of the South Church of Dundee, a faithful evangelical labourer in the Church of Scotland who contended for gospel truth against Erastian encroachment and the deadening formality of his age. He is remembered above all as a shepherd who fed his flock at the LORD’s Table, for his Sacramental Meditations and Advices and his Sacramental Catechism taught generations of communicants how to prepare their hearts, examine themselves, and feed upon Christ crucified with faith and reverence. Willison would have the Supper no bare form but a covenant feast, where the believer, mourning his sin and beholding the broken body and shed blood, closes afresh with the Saviour and rises strengthened for the pilgrimage. He wrote plainly and warmly for the common people, that the shepherd and the tradesman might come worthily to the sacrament and not eat and drink judgment to themselves; and his Afflicted Man’s Companion ministered the same Christ to the sickbed and the house of mourning. In a season when many pulpits grew moralistic and cold, Willison held up the cross, pressed personal godliness, and defended the crown rights of the Redeemer over His Church. His labour teaches that the sacrament rightly used is a means of grace, not a mere memorial gesture, and that faithful pastoral writing arms plain believers to draw near unto God.

etymology: English given name John, from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious”; with the surname Brown; distinguished by his charge at Haddington in East Lothian.
biblical_def: John Brown of Haddington (1722–1787) was a Scottish minister of the Secession Church whose life is a monument to the sovereign grace that lifts the lowly. Orphaned young and set to herd sheep, he taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and other tongues upon the hillside with a hunger for the Scriptures that shamed the learned, and was so remarkable in it that ignorant men once charged him with sorcery. Called to the ministry, he served the congregation at Haddington and was made Professor of Divinity to the Associate Synod, training a generation of preachers. His great labour was the Self-Interpreting Bible, in which he gathered marginal helps, notes, and cross-references that Scripture might expound Scripture and the plain reader be furnished to search the Word for himself; and his Dictionary of the Bible and Systematic Theology served the same end of putting sound doctrine into the hands of the common people. He wrote a dying address to his children charging them to seek the LORD, and left them, as he said, in the arms of a covenant God. His labour teaches that no station is too mean for the LORD to raise up a servant, that diligence in the Word is a holy calling, and that the surest commentary on the Bible is the Bible itself, rightly compared and believed.
webster_summary: Self-taught shepherd-scholar and Secession divine, author of the Self-Interpreting Bible.

etymology: Greek given name Andrew, from Andreas, “manly” or “strong”; with the Scottish surname Gray, from the colour, an ancient family name.
biblical_def: Andrew Gray (1633–1656) was a young minister of the Outer High Kirk of Glasgow whose brief flame the LORD lit and quenched within a few short years. Converted, it is said, by a beggar’s word that pierced his heart, he entered the ministry while yet very young and preached with such heavenly savour and searching power that great throngs pressed to hear him, though he was scarce more than a youth. He handled the great themes of the gospel—the freeness of grace, the worth of Christ, the necessity of the new birth, the believer’s access to God—with a fervour and unction beyond his years, so that his sermons, taken down and printed after his death, were treasured for their spiritual weight. He died at two-and-twenty, having preached but some two years, and yet he crowded into that little span a fulness of usefulness that shamed longer lives. His labour teaches that the LORD is not bound to length of days to accomplish His work, that He can make a mere youth mighty in the Scriptures, and that the power of preaching lies not in the years or the eloquence of the man but in the Spirit who takes the things of Christ and shows them to the soul. His early death preaches also that our times are in the LORD’s hand, and that faithfulness, not longevity, is the measure of a life.
webster_summary: Gifted young preacher of Glasgow who died at twenty-two, leaving sermons of rare spiritual power.

etymology: Germanic given name William, “resolute protector”; the middle name Chalmers honouring the family; with the Scottish surname Burns, from a dweller by a stream or burn.
biblical_def: William Chalmers Burns (1815–1868) was a Scottish evangelist and missionary whom the LORD honoured both in the revivals of his homeland and in the mission-field of China. In 1839, supplying the pulpit of Robert Murray M’Cheyne at Dundee while that saintly man was abroad, Burns saw the Spirit fall in mighty awakening at Kilsyth and Dundee, and multitudes were pierced under the plain preaching of the cross; yet he shunned the praise of men and sought only that Christ be magnified in the conversion of sinners. Constrained afterward to the regions beyond, he gave the labour of his later life to China, where he laboured obscurely and long, translating and preaching among a people not his own, adopting their dress and their ways that he might win some, and dying at last at Newchwang far from home, having as he said sought first the kingdom of God. He was a man of much prayer, of self-denial, of childlike dependence, careless of comfort and reputation, single in his aim to see souls born again. His labour teaches that revival is the sovereign work of the Spirit and not the contrivance of man, that the same gospel that awakens a Scottish town is the power of God unto a Chinese province, and that the missionary’s crown is faithfulness in obscurity, sowing in tears where another may reap.
webster_summary: Scottish revival preacher of Kilsyth and Dundee who became a self-denying missionary to China.

etymology: English given name John, “the LORD is gracious”; with the Highland surname Kennedy, from Gaelic Ceannaideach; distinguished by his charge at Dingwall in Ross-shire.
biblical_def: John Kennedy of Dingwall (1819–1884) was a Free Church minister of the Scottish Highlands, one of the great preachers of the North, who stood for the old evangelical religion of Ross-shire against the innovations and declensions of his day. Son of a godly minister and heir to the rich Highland tradition of experimental religion, he laboured at Dingwall with a searching, doctrinal, Christ-exalting ministry that fed the hungry and probed the false, dividing between the living and the dead among his hearers. In his best-loved book, The Days of the Fathers in Ross-shire, he embalmed the memory of the eminent men of God and the discerning Christians of the Highland past, that their spiritual wisdom and their experience of grace might not perish. He resisted hymns, instrumental music, and the moods of Moody’s methods where he judged them to loosen the old paths, and contended earnestly for the purity of worship and the sovereignty of grace. His labour teaches that a preacher must feed the flock with the whole counsel of God, distinguishing law and gospel and the marks of true grace from its counterfeits, and that the reverent memory of faithful forefathers is a means the LORD uses to hold a people to the truth once delivered. He is a pattern of the doctrinal, experimental, uncompromising Highland ministry.

etymology: Germanic given name William, “resolute protector”; with the Scottish surname Cunningham, from the district of Cunninghame in Ayrshire.
biblical_def: William Cunningham (1805–1861) was a Free Church of Scotland divine, one of the leaders of the Disruption of 1843, and Principal of New College, Edinburgh, whose massive learning was ever bent to the defence of the Reformed faith. A vigorous controversialist and a master of the history of doctrine, he stood with Chalmers and the evangelical party in the Ten Years’ Conflict and came out at the Disruption for the crown rights of Christ and the spiritual independence of the Church, forsaking manse and stipend rather than bow the Church’s Head to the civil power. His enduring service to the Church lay in his teaching and writing, above all his Historical Theology, in which he traced the great doctrines through the councils, the Reformation, and the confessions, exposing error and vindicating the truth of grace with the eye of a lawyer and the heart of a believer. He honoured the Reformers as recoverers of the gospel from Rome’s corruptions and defended justification by faith, election, and the finished work of Christ against every rising subtlety. His labour teaches that the history of the Church is a field of battle for the truth, that doctrine matters unto salvation, and that a scholar’s learning is best spent, not in cold speculation, but in the defence of the faith once delivered and the honour of the Redeemer’s crown.
webster_summary: Free Church divine and Disruption leader, author of Historical Theology.

etymology: Greek given name George, from georgos, “husbandman” or “tiller of the earth”; with the Scottish surname Smeaton, a place-name.
biblical_def: George Smeaton (1814–1889) was a Free Church of Scotland divine and Professor of New Testament Exegesis at New College, Edinburgh, a close friend of Robert Murray M’Cheyne and one of the most exact and reverent expositors of his generation. His great gift to the Church was to gather the very words of the LORD Jesus and of His apostles upon the central mysteries of the faith and to let Scripture speak. In The Doctrine of the Atonement as Taught by Christ Himself and its companion volume on the teaching of the apostles, he set forth the substitutionary sacrifice of Christ—that the Son of Man came to give His life a ransom for many, bearing the sins of His people in His own body on the tree, and satisfying the justice of God—against every scheme that would soften the cross into a mere example or a governmental display. He wrote likewise a full and rich treatise on the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, following the same exact, exegetical, God-honouring method. His labour teaches that the atonement is penal and substitutionary at its heart, that Christ bore the wrath our sins deserved and purchased a definite redemption for His own, and that the surest theology is that which sits humbly under the plain teaching of Christ and His apostles rather than reasoning above the Word.

etymology: English given name James, from the Hebrew Ya’aqov (Jacob), “supplanter” or “heel-holder”; with the Scottish surname Buchanan, from the lands of Buchanan by Loch Lomond.
biblical_def: James Buchanan (1804–1870) was a Free Church of Scotland divine who succeeded Thomas Chalmers as Professor of Divinity at New College, Edinburgh, and gave to the Church one of the great expositions of the article by which she stands or falls. In his The Doctrine of Justification, delivered as the Cunningham Lectures, he traced the doctrine through the Scriptures and through the history of the Church, showing how the gospel of a free righteousness was recovered at the Reformation and guarding it against the corruptions of Rome, the errors of the Socinians, and every scheme that would mingle the sinner’s works with the finished righteousness of Christ. He taught, with the Reformers and the confessions, that justification is a judicial act of God whereby He pardons the sinner and accounts him righteous, not for anything wrought in him or done by him, but solely for the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith alone. His labour teaches that justification by faith is no peripheral matter but the very heart of the gospel and the ground of a sinner’s peace, that the righteousness which saves is Christ’s and not our own, and that the Church must guard this doctrine with unsleeping vigilance, for wherever it is obscured the light of the gospel itself grows dim.

etymology: Germanic given name Hugh, from hug, “heart, mind, spirit”; with the surname Martin, from the Latin Martinus, related to Mars, the god of war.
biblical_def: Hugh Martin (1822–1885) was a Free Church of Scotland minister and theologian, trained in mathematics before he was given to the ministry, whose keen and ordered mind was consecrated to the deep things of the gospel. Compelled by ill health to lay down his pastoral charge, he gave his later years to writing, and in The Atonement—in its relations to the covenant, the priesthood, and the intercession of our Lord—he set forth with rare vigour the federal, substitutionary work of Christ, showing how the cross flows out of the eternal covenant of grace and is bound up with Christ’s priestly office and His unceasing intercession for those He redeemed. He would not let the atonement stand as a bare transaction but wove it into the whole counsel of God, that the shed blood and the pleading Advocate are one work for one people. His treatise on Jonah, reading that prophet as a type of Christ, breathes the same reverent, Christ-centred exposition. His labour teaches that the death of Christ is a definite, covenant redemption, that the Priest who died yet lives to intercede, and that the surest comfort of the believer is to know his sins were laid on a Substitute appointed in the everlasting covenant, whose finished sacrifice and living intercession together secure the salvation of all for whom He died.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved because Martin’s labour rebukes every scheme that would sever the cross from the covenant and the priesthood, whether by making the atonement a general and indefinite thing or by dividing Christ’s dying from His living intercession.

The principle to recover is the federal, substitutionary, and definite atonement of Christ—flowing from the everlasting covenant, wrought by His priestly sacrifice, and secured by His unceasing intercession—which is the sure ground of the believer’s comfort.
